6.a: (1) Materials — an incense stick, a matchbox and a room with still air, (2) Procedure — light the incense stick in one corner and let the fragrance spread through the room, (3) Observation — the fragrance, the solute gas, mixes uniformly with the air, the solvent gas, within minutes and shows no separation, (4) Homogeneity proof — the uniform single-phase spread of the solute gas through the solvent gas is observable diffusion, exactly what defines a gaseous solution. A poor answer such as mixing two gases in a jar lacks a practical demonstration of homogeneity and does not use observable diffusion.

2.a: (1) Result — the solution becomes unsaturated, (2) Le Chatelier reasoning — dissolution of ammonium nitrate is endothermic, so heat acts as a reactant and raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward more dissolution, (3) Consequence — solubility at the higher temperature is greater, so the previously saturated solution can dissolve more solid and is unsaturated against the new higher limit, (4) Contrast — a supersaturated solution only arises when a hot saturated solution cools without crystallisation. A common error is to think heating always makes solutions supersaturated.

6.a: (1) Materials — a potato, a knife, two bowls, water, sugar and a scale, (2) Procedure — cut four identical potato cylinders, weigh them, keep two in pure water and two in saturated sugar solution for half an hour, then blot and reweigh, (3) Observation — cylinders in water gain mass and turn turgid while cylinders in the sugar solution lose mass by plasmolysis, (4) Estimating osmotic pressure — plotting percent mass change against sugar concentration locates the isotonic point of zero change, and near room temperature a 0.3 molar sugar solution is about isotonic with plant cell sap, giving roughly 7.4 bar. A poor answer uses dialysis tubing, which is not a household material, or a thistle-funnel column, while the potato method shows the core principle that water moves toward the higher solute concentration.

5.a: (1) Verdict — the student's name is incorrect, (2) The rule — when the coordination sphere is an anion, the metal name must take the -ate suffix, (3) Correct name — potassium tetrachloridopalladate(II), (4) The trap — using the elemental metal name for an anionic coordination entity is the classic board-exam error, with only a few metals keeping Latin-based names such as ferrate, cuprate and argentate. A student who writes palladium(II) for the anionic complex has not applied the anion -ate rule.

(1) Verdict — the student's postfix ABCD^*+E- is correct, (2) The trace — A is output, plus is pushed, B is output, star is pushed above plus, C is output, caret is pushed above star, D is output, (3) Meeting the minus — caret is popped, then star, then plus, because minus shares the lowest precedence and equal-precedence operators pop for left-to-right associativity, so the minus is pushed and popped after E, (4) The logic — precedence decides when an operator leaves the stack and associativity decides ties. A wrong answer claiming the conversion is incorrect reveals misunderstanding of the precedence hierarchy or of associativity.
